# Population, prosperity and recovery

Sustained paid food and purchasing power shape bounded city welfare\.

Prosperity is a 0 to 100 indicator, not a cash or price multiplier\. Up to six recent scheduled food opportunities, including failures to buy, supply a paid\-fulfillment share\. Current household cash is compared with a reserve benchmark for the next Bread need, priced exactly using current parameters and a hypothetical shelf containing at least that need\. This is not a future availability or price promise\. Three parts fulfillment and one part purchasing power set the target; prosperity moves toward it by at most three points per observation\.

Furniture demand turns on after three consecutive qualifying observations with prosperity at least 65 and full food plus an affordable next\-need reserve\. It turns off after three consecutive observations with prosperity at most 40 or purchasing power below 25 percent\. This hysteresis prevents daily threshold flicker; demand remains subject to real stock and budgets\.

Population reviews occur every 12 days after six food observations\. At most one resident is gained after sustained adequate food and prosperity at least 65, or lost after sustained severe deprivation and prosperity at most 35\. Generated bounds are 10 to 80\. New population changes subsequent desired need, not past records\.

A city can keep household money yet decline because food is absent; another may have food but no purchasing power\. Production inputs, payroll, market buying power and transport can all stall a chain\. The model has no guaranteed long\-run equilibrium\. Grand Commission welfare cards test sustained paid food against the declared baseline, not a one\-time shipment\.
